Whereof
hwâr-ov'
adv. (compound relative; rendering Hebrew 'asher with a suffix, Greek relative pronouns in the genitive)
A compound of where and of, meaning of which or of whom. The where- compounds are the relative counterparts of the there- compounds: thereof points back to a thing already named, whereof introduces the clause that describes it.

Biblical Definition

Whereof means of which, and it does the work of a relative pronoun with a preposition attached. It appears in the LORD's recital of His own commandment in Eden: “the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat” (Genesis 3:11), the clause defining precisely which tree and precisely what was said. Joshua uses it to identify the cities of refuge as a promise already made and now executed: “Appoint out for you cities of refuge, whereof I spake unto you by the hand of Moses” (Joshua 20:2). Paul uses it before Felix to demand the ordinary standard of evidence: “Neither can they prove the things whereof they now accuse me” (Acts 24:13) — a Christian appealing, rightly, to Roman rules of proof. And he uses it of his own office: “Whereof I was made a minister, according to the gift of the grace of God given unto me by the effectual working of his power” (Ephesians 3:7). The psalmist uses it for the river of God: “There is a river, the streams whereof shall make glad the city of God” (Psalm 46:4).

Webster 1828 Definition

A compound adverb meaning of which or of whom; the relative counterpart of thereof. In Scripture it identifies the thing spoken of — the tree whereof God commanded, the cities whereof He spake, the charges whereof Paul was accused.

expand to see more

WHEREOF, adv. [where and of.] Of which; of whom.

2. It introduces a relative clause, and answers to thereof, which refers backward.

3. It belongs to the class of compound relatives: whereof, whereby, wherein, wherewith, whereunto.

4. It is retained chiefly in the legal and scriptural style.

5. In Scripture, the tree, whereof I commanded thee, Gen. 3; the things whereof they now accuse me, Acts 24.

Key Scripture

Genesis 3:11 — "And he said, Who told thee that thou wast naked? Hast thou eaten of the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat?"

Joshua 20:2 — "Speak to the children of Israel, saying, Appoint out for you cities of refuge, whereof I spake unto you by the hand of Moses:"

Acts 24:13 — "Neither can they prove the things whereof they now accuse me."

Ephesians 3:7 — "Whereof I was made a minister, according to the gift of the grace of God given unto me by the effectual working of his power."

Modern Corruption

Paul's demand that his accusers prove their charges is a standing rebuke to accusation by assertion — the trial by reputation that flourishes wherever a claim is treated as established the moment it is made.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle needing recovery is the biblical law of witnesses. Scripture requires two or three, provides for the examination of them, and prescribes that a false witness receive the penalty he sought for his brother. Paul stands on this before Felix: neither can they prove the things whereof they now accuse me. The church has the same rule for its own courts — against an elder receive not an accusation, but before two or three witnesses — a protection that exists precisely because accusations against ministers are easy to make and ruinous to answer.

The rule protects two parties at once, and both halves must be kept. It protects the accused from ruin by rumour; it also requires that credible charges actually be heard, since the same passage that guards the elder commands that those who sin be rebuked before all. A congregation that will not hear evidence against a man it admires has broken the law of witnesses as surely as one that condemns without any. Justice in Scripture is neither indulgent nor credulous; it examines.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew has one indeclinable relative, 'asher, whose case is supplied by a resumptive pronoun later in the clause; Greek declines its relative hos and puts it in the genitive for whereof.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'asher (H834) — who, which, that; an indeclinable relative whose sense is fixed by the clause.

Greek hou (G3739) — of which or of whom; the genitive of the relative pronoun.

Greek apodeiknumi (G584) — to prove or demonstrate; the verb Paul's accusers could not satisfy.

Hebrew miqlat (H4733) — a refuge or asylum; the cities appointed in Joshua 20:2.

Greek diakonos (G1249) — a servant or minister; what Paul was made of the gospel in Ephesians 3:7.

Usage

"Of the precise commandment recalled in Eden: the tree, whereof I commanded thee that thou shouldest not eat (Genesis 3:11)."

"Of a promise now being executed: cities of refuge, whereof I spake unto you by the hand of Moses (Joshua 20:2)."

"Of charges that could not be proved: Neither can they prove the things whereof they now accuse me (Acts 24:13)."
